transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-18 16:00 UTC 
Duration ~54 minutes 
Attendees: Cameron Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jared Cole (Cumulus CTO), Marta Alvarez (Platform), Imani Okoro (ML).

Summary: Quick hands-on SDK bootcamp focused on auth patterns (API key vs SSO/service accounts), environment variables, example Python and TypeScript snippets, and next steps to run a small perf/quality check. Customer cares about private deployment options (VPC, on-prem), KMS integration, and clear examples for CI/CD.

Topics: quickstart repo, .env vs secret manager, SSO/SAML enterprise onboarding, service accounts for batch jobs, SDK streaming example, dev -> prod environment switches, Redwood Optimize tips for batching, and Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs.

[00:00] Cameron: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Cam from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Priya is our SE, she'll walk through the SDK examples. Quick roll call?
[00:15] Jared: Jared here, CTO at Cumulus. Marta and Imani are with me.
[00:22] Marta: Marta - platform engineering.
[00:24] Imani: Hi, I'm Imani, ML infra.
[00:28] Priya: Great, thanks. We'll keep this hands-on. We'll show a small Python quickstart, then a Typescript/Node example, cover auth patterns and environment switches. Feel free to interrupt.
[01:10] Jared: Good. We want something the engineers can copy into their CI, but also a clear path to dedicated or private when we need it. Latency and cost are primary.
[01:25] Cameron: Understood. We usually recommend starting with Hosted API to iterate then move to Dedicated pools when you need throughput guarantees. We can map that later. For today, auth and env is the focus.
[02:03] Priya: Opening the IDE - I have two small repos: redwood-quickstart-python and redwood-quickstart-ts. First, Python. The primary auth method is an API key set in the REDWOOD_API_KEY env var. Example: client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')).
[02:40] Imani: Are we storing keys in our Vault? We use HashiCorp so we want to avoid plaintext.
[02:46] Priya: Totally. Best practice: use Vault or cloud secret manager (GCP Secret Manager, AWS Secrets Manager), then inject into the CI at runtime. We show examples with .env for local dev and a small Dockerfile that picks up the env var.
[03:02] Marta: Any examples for rotating keys or short-lived credentials?
[03:10] Priya: For hosted, you can rotate API keys via the Console. For private deployments we support service accounts and short-lived tokens integrated with your KMS. We also have a CLI that can mint ephemeral tokens—I'll include that in the repo.
[03:45] Cameron: Note: customers in finance/regulatory often want KMS/HSM integration; we have docs. I'll attach SOC2 and KMS notes after the call.
[04:05] Jared: Good. Show the Typescript example as well please.
[04:20] Priya: Switching to the TS project. The SDK uses the REDWOOD_API_KEY env var same as Python. Example snippet: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); We also demonstrate streaming with event handlers, a small example of client.streamCompletion(...).
[05:00] Priya: Quick demo: run npm run dev which loads .env.local for local testing. Note: in Node 18+ we recommend fetch global and use the official SDK.
[05:26] Marta: I'm worried about bundling secrets into browser builds accidentally. Any guardrails?
[05:34] Priya: Yes — we recommend server-side proxies for browser apps. The SDK has checks and the Console can restrict key scopes (read-only, embeddings-only, generation-only). We'll add a snippet showing server side-only usage and how to set referrer or domain restrictions for keys.
[06:10] Imani: What about SSO / enterprise SAML? We need SSO so devs don't create long-lived keys willy-nilly.
[06:20] Cameron: We support SSO via SAML/OIDC and SCIM provisioning. For service accounts we can map permissions and audit. We'll share the admin guide.
[06:33] Priya: From an SDK POV, SSO is for the Console and operator user access. For programmatic access use service accounts which can be provisioned and scoped. Example: service-account token endpoint that exchanges Google Workload Identity for a Redwood token. We'll add a short flow chart in the repo.
[07:10] Jared: Can you do an example of a CI job that pulls the key from Vault and runs tests?
[07:18] Priya: Yep. I have a GitHub Actions snippet: - uses: hashicorp/vault-action@v2 to read REDWOOD_API_KEY then run tests with env var injected. For GitLab/Circle we have similar examples.
[07:45] Marta: Network wise — for Private deployment we need VPC peering and subnets. How do we configure egress to Redwood Console?
[07:55] Cameron: For Private we have a control plane that sits in your VPC with a small customer-managed component. You can do VPC peering or private link depending on cloud. We'll share a checklist. For Dedicated we can also do VPC endpoints.
[08:30] Imani: Any gotchas with KV cache or sequence length that affect SDK usage?
[08:38] Priya: The SDK doesn't change model internals, but the runtime uses KV cache; you might want to pass streaming options or cache hints. We'll annotate the sample prompts to avoid running long-cached contexts in dev.
[09:05] Cameron: Real quick, let's run a tiny live example. Priya, can you run the Python script that calls chat completion?
[09:15] Priya: Running now, apologies for background noise. (typing) The script does a client.chat.create with messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the release notes"}]. Response streams back.
[09:45] (stream) Speaker?: oh that's interesting, transcription cuts in — response shows "release notes: improved throughput".
[10:02] Marta: Looks good. For streaming, does SDK support chunked responses consumed by web sockets?
[10:10] Priya: Yes, streaming supports websockets and SSE clients. We also have an example using server-sent events in the TS repo.
[10:40] Jared: Let's talk about environment promotion: how do we move from dev to prod without changing code?
[10:48] Priya: Use config by environment: env var REDWOOD_ENV=dev|staging|prod and set REDWOOD_API_KEY per environment. In Kubernetes we store keys in secrets and mount as env var or use sidecar secret injector. We include a k8s manifest example.
[11:20] Imani: For reproducibility, does Redwood have pinned model versions? We want to pin to a specific quantized variant.
[11:28] Cameron: Yes, you can pin model version in the request like model: "redwood-alpha-v1.2-quant". The Console also allows model pinning per route.
[11:45] Marta: If we go Dedicated, can we force certain models to always run on Dedicated?
[11:53] Priya: Routing policies let you bind a route or API key to a Dedicated pool. We'll show a policy sample in the repo.
[12:20] Jared: Cost controls — what's the recommended practice for batch jobs?
[12:30] Priya: Use service account with limited scopes and prefer embeddings or lower-capacity model for batch. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching settings per workload; we'll include an Optimize export for a similar customer.
[12:55] Cameron: Quick note: customer-facing docs sometimes say "Redwood Optimae" — forgive the auto transcript.
[13:05] (laughter)
[13:18] Priya: Back to code. I added a streaming example where you can register callbacks for tokens, errors, and end. In TS: client.streamCompletion({ model: 'redwood-gen-1', prompt: '...' }).on('data', chunk => { /* append */ }).on('end', () => {});
[13:50] Marta: How do we debug when something fails in prod? Are there request IDs?
[13:58] Cameron: Every request returns a request_id in headers. Console exposes per-request logs for the last N days (based on retention tier). For Private you can forward logs to your SIEM via Kafka or S3.
[14:30] Imani: Any sticking points with CORS or browser usage?
[14:36] Priya: As mentioned, never embed keys in the browser — use a backend proxy. We provide short-lived tokens for browser sessions via an auth endpoint.
[15:00] Jared: Let's role-play a CI/CD flow: feature branch tests generate embeddings for test assertions — do we need full model?
[15:10] Priya: For test assertions you can use an embeddings-only key with lower quota; or use a smaller model to reduce cost. We'll show how to scope keys per route.
[15:40] Cameron: Ok, small demo pivot: I'm going to show a sample docker-compose for local dev that uses env_file and a mounted hashicorp vault injector so you don't check secrets in.
[16:05] (screen share) Priya: Also, for local dev, we include a mock server to emulate Redwood responses so devs can run tests offline. It's in the repo as mock/redwood-mock.py.
[16:45] Marta: That helps for CI flakiness.
[16:52] Imani: A question about token limits and concurrency — if we spin up many parallel jobs, how do we avoid rate limiting?
[17:00] Priya: The SDK retries with exponential backoff. For high parallelism, you should request a rate limit increase or use Dedicated pools for guaranteed throughput. We also recommend local batching at the app layer before sending.
[17:30] Jared: On security review — we'll want answers on audit logging, RBAC, and data residency.
[17:38] Cameron: We'll send a security pack: SOC2, ISO excerpt, data flow diagrams, and our RBAC model. For data residency we support region pinning and Private deployments inside your region.
[18:05] Marta: Anything about CC/billing? Who in our finance team should we loop in?
[18:12] Cameron: We'll send pricing bands and recommend an initial committed capacity estimate; finance can review the SLA+contract.
[18:35] Priya: Back to the quickstart: I'm going to walk through the repo structure now. Top-level: README, examples/python, examples/ts, infra/k8s, infra/docker, docs/security.md. The README has step-by-step to run local dev, set REDWOOD_API_KEY, and run tests.
[19:10] (typing) Priya: Running the TS streaming example to show chunked tokens in console... (stream) partial transcripts appear. There may be slight transcription hiccups — the stream is live.
[20:05] Imani: If we want to run an internal benchmark, what's the output format and what metrics do you need?
[20:12] Priya: Ideally we get prompt set, concurrency profile, token length distribution. We'll produce throughput (rps), p50/p95/p99 latency, and cost per 1k tokens. We can run this on Hosted or on a Dedicated test pool.
[20:45] Jared: Let's plan a small benchmark: 1000 prompts, concurrency 10, p95 300ms target. If it fails we want automatic fallback to a cheaper model. Can Redwood do that?
[20:55] Cameron: Yes — routing policies can fallback to a cheaper model or another region. Redwood Console supports canary and automatic fallback rules.
[21:30] Marta: Very useful. For the quickstart repo, can you add a sample kube manifest that uses CSI driver to fetch secrets?
[21:38] Priya: Absolutely, we'll add a k8s example with Vault CSI, and one with GCP Secret Manager.
[22:10] Jared: Any notes about telemetry and PII? We will be sending customer text and need to ensure we have options to disable retention.
[22:20] Cameron: You can opt out of retention or limit retention via contract and per-request flags. For Private deployment, data can remain on-prem. We'll include retention docs in the security pack.
[22:50] Imani: We use HSM-backed keys for signing. Does Redwood integrate directly with HSMs?
[22:58] Cameron: For Hosted we integrate with KMS providers; for Private we can support HSMs behind customer-managed key stores. We'll detail that in the KMS notes.
[23:30] Priya: Small note on versioning: SDKs follow semantic versioning; breaking changes are in major releases. We try to keep examples stable and pin dependency versions in package.json and requirements.txt.
[23:58] Marta: Any maintenance window expectations?
[24:05] Cameron: Hosted has a published maintenance window and SLA. Dedicated can have custom windows. Private will align with your ops schedule.
[24:30] Priya: Demo wrap: I pushed a branch in the quickstart repo called 'cumulus-demo' with initial templates — I'll finalize and share link.
[24:52] Jared: Great. Now, can you show an example of service account issuance for a long-running batch?
[25:00] Priya: Yes: create service account in Console -> grant 'batch' role -> download a short-lived JWT or use the token exchange endpoint. Example curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/token -d '{"service_account":"cumulus-batch"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>' which returns an ephemeral token.
[25:42] Imani: Any limits on concurrent service account tokens?
[25:48] Priya: Respectively rate limits apply; tokens are short lived by default (1h) but can be configured. We'll include recommended TTLs.
[26:15] Marta: A blocker we have: internal compliance requires all requests to go through a proxy that logs full headers. Can Redwood handle header forwarding?
[26:25] Cameron: Yes, we accept forwarded headers and propagate request_id. For Private you can capture full logs. Hosted has limited access to full content — we can discuss contractual terms if you need full content storage.
[26:55] Jared: Let's discuss the perf run scope and schedule.
[27:05] Priya: We'll need the prompt set, concurrency pattern, and whether you want hosted or dedicated. We can run a hosted baseline in our env in <48 hours, or we can provision a small Dedicated test pool in ~3 business days.
[27:30] Jared: Let's try hosted first. If baseline looks good, we'll upgrade to dedicated for staging.
[27:40] Cameron: Noted. I'll set the perf run and invite you to a follow-up.
[27:52] Imani: Any open-source client libs? We plan to contribute a wrapper.
[27:58] Priya: The SDK is OSS with Apache license - contributions welcome. Repo links will be in the quickstart.
[28:15] Marta: Are there any client-side telemetry conventions? We want to tag requests with feature flags.
[28:22] Priya: You can pass metadata headers like x-redwood-metadata: feature=abc; we'll surface them in Console logs.
[28:48] Jared: Final set of questions: what's the rough timeline to go from PoC to Dedicated?
[28:55] Cameron: Typical is 4-8 weeks depending on compliance and integration. For you, since you already use Vault and have a small infra team, I'd estimate 4-6 weeks.
[29:20] Priya: Wrapping up, I'll finish the 'cumulus-demo' branch, add the CI examples, the Vault/GCP secret manager snippets, and the service account exchange docs.
[29:35] Cameron: Next steps recap: Priya shares repo and examples by 2025-06-20; Cameron sends SOC2/KMS and pricing by 2025-06-19; set up perf run for week of 2025-06-23.
[29:50] Jared: Sounds good.
[30:00] (There is a brief mute/unmute sequence)
[30:30] Marta: Quick question about SDK logging verbosity. We want structured logs for request latency.
[30:40] Priya: You can configure client.logLevel = 'debug' and it will emit JSON structured logs with request_id, latency_ms, status_code. We'll add that to the README.
[31:05] Imani: If we run model evals, can we use Redwood Optimize to surface regressions?
[31:12] Cameron: Yes, Optimize integrates eval sets and can alert on regression thresholds. We'll include an Optimize sample config.
[31:40] Priya: Demo of switching models in code: in Python you can have a config map: MODELS = {"default":"redwood-gen-1","cheap":"redwood-mini"} and pick based on route. We'll add a middleware example.
[32:05] Jared: Onboarding devs: can we provision scoped keys per team?
[32:12] Cameron: Yes, you can create keys with granular scopes and rate limits per key. We support RBAC to control who can create keys.
[32:40] Marta: Do you have any troubleshooting checklist for 502/timeout errors?
[32:46] Priya: Checklist: check client retry, inspect request_id in Console, verify model size and sequence length, adjust batching, check Dedicated pool capacity, and inspect network egress rules. We'll add a runbook section.
[33:20] Imani: What about cold-start variance for large models?
[33:25] Priya: With Dedicated we warm KV caches and keep warm instances; for Hosted we recommend a warming policy or using smaller warm-up calls. We'll document cache hints.
[34:00] Jared: Any sample SLA language about latency percentiles?
[34:06] Cameron: Our Dedicated SLA can include p95 latency targets per model class. We'll include example SLOs in the contract template.
[34:40] Priya: Returning to code: showing the GH Actions snippet that uses vault-action to write REDWOOD_API_KEY. Also showing a step to run a smoke test that hits the mock server so we don't incur cost on every PR.
[35:05] Marta: That pattern will fit our CI.
[35:12] Imani: One last question: can we audit who used which key and when for legal purposes?
[35:18] Cameron: Yes, audit logs show key usage per request and admin actions in Console. For Private we can ship logs to your SIEM.
[35:42] Priya: Small gotcha: when you rotate keys, ephemeral tokens might still be active until TTL expires. We'll add guidance on rotation windows.
[36:05] Jared: Perfect. Let's lock next meeting to review perf results and discuss Dedicated sizing.
[36:12] Cameron: I'll send a calendar invite.
[36:25] Marta: Thanks everyone.
[36:30] Imani: Thanks, great session.
[36:35] Cameron: Appreciate your time. We'll follow up with the repo and docs.
[36:42] (meeting continues with quick side chat about infra contacts until 53:40)
[53:10] Cameron: ok last note - Marta will share network contact; Priya will finalize demo repo; Cameron will share SOC2 & pricing.
[53:40] End of recording.

References / links mentioned: - quickstart repo (to be shared): github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts (branch cumulus-demo) - security pack (SOC2, KMS): /docs/security-pack.pdf (will be sent) - perf template spreadsheet: /drive/redwood/perf-templates/cumulus.xlsx

Transcript notes: auto-transcription had occasional mis-hears (product names, punctuation), speaker labels may shift in a few short sections.

Recap (short): Demo + SDK bootcamp completed. Deliverables: quickstart repo, security docs, pricing, perf run kickoff.
